On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. Training Qwen3.5-4B with ArgGYM's verifiers as rewards more than doubles complete-task success on held-out instances, with the largest gains on constructive tasks.

title: FAER: A Negative-Result Audit of Offline Trajectory Replay Selection on GSM8K
authors: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Tianshu Fu, Daren Zha
abstract: Offline trajectory replay selects model-generated reasoning traces from a frozen cache for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), yet cache-side answer correctness need not predict downstream accuracy on unseen problems. We report a failure-retaining audit of offline response SFT on GSM8K with Qwen3-1.7B fp16 LoRA over a frozen 384-row cache (256 training rows and 128 excluded held-out rows). Across three seeds (13, 17, 23) on a 256-problem test split, all three 32-row replay rules (uniform, format-feedback, and feedback-aware) obtain mean strict accuracies (0.7786, 0.7682, and 0.7956) below the no-update base model (0.8008), and every paired 95% confidence interval spans zero. Selector ranking is post-hoc unidentified (3 completed selectors versus the repaired protocol's minimum of 5, with rank correlation spanning both signs). Under an 8,192-supervised-token windowed schedule, 9 of 12 runs halt under calibration drift or unresolved nonfinite training loss or gradients, leaving only full-cache replay completed at 0.7721. A repaired campaign with dynamic loss scaling halted at its learning-rate pilot under reference-solution loss drift before accessing the 346-problem locked test split. Because the gold-rationale positive control was never executed, these negative results cannot separate cache quality, selector quality, and learner-protocol limits. Our one positive finding separates parser repair from prompt changes on a 64-problem audit split: reparsing fixed base generations with a Decimal extractor raises parse rate from 0.8750 to 1.0000 and accuracy from 0.7344 to 0.8281, whereas appending a format suffix flips 0.2500 of canonical answers. A preregistered replication on 512 fresh GSM8K training problems reproduces this parser-only gain (+8.40 pp, 95% CI [+6.05, +10.94]) for this checkpoint. We contribute a ledger-traceable negative-result record and 9 lessons learned.

title: Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models
authors: Andrei Marchenko, Viacheslav Bezrukov, Oleg Kashurin, Inessa Fedorova, Dmitry Bocharov, Yuliana Shakhvalieva, Maria Tikhonova, Valerii Ternovskii
abstract: Looped language models increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, but existing large-scale recipes require multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, while the benefits of recurrence remain difficult to separate from differences in data and training. In this work, we establish practical training recipes for looped language models, with three main results. (1) We develop a compute-efficient from-scratch pipeline that reduces the training budget from 7.7T tokens in Ouro to 310B tokens while retaining strong reasoning performance. Pretraining followed by high-quality mid-training, together with learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization, enables stable recurrent training without prior multi-stage schedules. (2) Under controlled comparisons, our 1.4B LoopLM outperforms a parameter-matched dense model trained on the same data and token budget on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, including +14 points on GSM8K, +10 on MATH, and +22 on DROP. At matched inference compute, it approaches a 3.9B dense model on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension while using only 36\% as many parameters. (3) We introduce a minimal recipe for converting pretrained dense models into looped ones: a single learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, with no step-specific parameters. Applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Looped Qwen improves over an identically continued dense baseline on every evaluated benchmark across two data regimes, with statistically clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro on the curated mixture. Together, these results make looped language models substantially cheaper to train from scratch and practical to introduce into existing pretrained checkpoints, while isolating the gains due to recurrence itself.

title: Latent Information Sharing for Accelerating Federated Learning
authors: Seungjun Lee, Ensieh Khazaei, Dimitrios Hatzinakos, Baturalp Buyukates, Sunwoo Lee
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a communication-efficient distributed learning paradigm. However, client drift remains one of the most critical challenges, hindering the efficient training of a global model. In this study, we propose a novel latent information sharing scheme that directly mitigates data heterogeneity across clients. Our theoretical and empirical results show that sharing a small amount of hidden-layer activations significantly improves training efficiency while preserving convergence guarantees and data privacy. Furthermore, we compare our method with existing FL approaches designed to address client drift, including FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedPVR, FedProto, and SplitFed, and demonstrate superior model accuracy under a fixed round budget without incurring excessive communication overhead. Overall, this work presents a promising new knowledge aggregation scheme and provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of activation sharing on federated optimization.

title: From Redundancy to Minimality: Fixed-Point-Guided Hierarchical Reduction of Learned Piecewise-Linear Dynamics
authors: Hiroto Tamura, Gouhei Tanaka
abstract: Understanding a nonlinear dynamical system from time series requires not only reproducing its trajectories, but also identifying a simple representation that preserves its essential dynamical structure. Almost-linear recurrent neural networks (AL-RNNs) are piecewise-linear RNNs in which only a subset of units use ReLU nonlinearities, so that nonlinear capacity is explicitly controlled by the number of ReLU units. Their activation patterns define linear regions, represented as symbols, whose observed transitions form a symbolic transition graph. However, directly training AL-RNNs with few ReLU units to realize minimal dynamical representations can be unreliable. We ask whether an AL-RNN with more ReLU units can instead be trained first and systematically reduced to a minimal dynamical representation. We introduce a fixed-point-guided hierarchical reduction procedure that progressively linearizes selected ReLU units, merging neighboring linear regions and graph nodes while preserving distinct symbols containing fixed points (FPs). The resulting reduction tree defines a hierarchy of progressively simpler candidates. Each reduced candidate is initialized from the parent parameters and retrained through gradual linearization with guidance from the parent dynamics. We also prove that, under certain assumptions, reproducing $Q$ distinct fixed points requires at least $Q$ FP-containing symbols, providing a certificate of symbol-level minimality when this bound is attained. Across six tasks spanning attractor reconstruction and flip-flop memory, our learn-reduce-retrain strategy substantially improves the recovery of minimal models, including settings where direct training rarely succeeds. These results show that redundant nonlinear capacity can serve as a scaffold for discovering and realizing minimal dynamical representations.

title: Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing
authors: Shiwei Tan, Huzefa Rangwala, Danielle C. Maddix
abstract: High-fidelity simulations are essential to scientific and engineering design, but can be expensive to run repeatedly. Learned surrogates offer a faster alternative, yet their higher errors may alter downstream decisions. This accuracy-speed tradeoff creates a need to determine whether a surrogate can be used or the full simulator remains necessary. We study decisions determined by whether a scalar quantity of interest lies above or below a fixed threshold. For each input, we use the surrogate when its conformal interval lies entirely on one side of the threshold and route the input to simulation when the interval intersects it. Standard conformal prediction constructs intervals without reference to the downstream decision threshold: even a narrow interval near the threshold can cross it and trigger simulation, whereas a wider interval farther away can remain entirely on one side and require no simulation. We introduce Threshold-Aware Conformal Routing (TACR), which learns an input-dependent scale using a threshold-aware objective that concentrates interval tightness near the decision boundary. Exact split-conformal calibration on held-out data preserves distribution-free marginal coverage, which also upper-bounds the probability of an incorrect threshold decision that is not routed. Across various scientific and engineering datasets, TACR reduces simulator deferrals by 14-75% relative to standard conformal prediction at the same coverage target. Against a variant without threshold-local weighting but with similar predictor accuracy, TACR further reduces deferrals by 10-24% on four datasets. These results show that optimizing interval allocation for routing can reduce simulator calls without weakening the standard conformal guarantee.

title: RouteAudit: A Negative Result on Adaptive Multi-Verifier Routing under Matched Fixed-Subset Controls
authors: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Tianshu Fu, Daren Zha
abstract: Apparent savings from adaptive verifier routing can come from a fixed verifier subset. We audit GSM8K using cached Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-2B candidates paired with Qwen3-4B, three LLM verifiers, 1,319 held-out requests, and 5 router seeds. Our shared-fusion audit compares routers with the complete fixed-subset envelope, including zero-call abstention, under matched prices and scoring. Calibration-selected single-call verification matches full static verification in 3 of 4 cells. In a separate comparison using the original fusion rules and two-verifier catalog, archived learned and offline-RL routers lose 0.038 to 0.171 in quality against matched static SF+SA. Across 480 budget-matched offline fits in six router families, the family envelope gain is zero in each cell at the primary price. No locked router obtains a positive simultaneous bootstrap lower bound across 68 cell-by-price points. None is classified as complete-static dominant, and all 4 primary-price points are inconclusive. At the primary price, the tested-family gain upper bound is at most 0.002. The oracle headroom upper bound is 0.034 to 0.045, above our 0.01 margin, leaving meaningful gains open. At 45 of 64 grid points excluding the primary price, the oracle lower bound exceeds 0.01 and the tested-family upper bound is at most 0.01. Coverage of these envelope bounds remains unverified. At a true gain of 0.03, the procedure rejects on 44.1% of points, and planted-effect family coverage ranges from 0.923 to 0.931. We report lessons from this catalog.

title: NeuroLens: Learning Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics from Chronic Recordings
authors: Hanrui Lyu, Baiyuan Chen, Tianshu Tan, Matthew R. Whiteway, Maxwell D. Melin, Ji Xia, Linyang He, Bradly C. Stadie, Anne Churchland, Liam Paninski, Yizi Zhang
abstract: Understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve during learning is a central pursuit in neuroscience. However, tracking meaningful representational changes remains challenging because recorded neural populations change across days. Here, we introduce NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics), a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (LeJEPA). An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, where a temporal predictor forecasts future latent states. Across mouse and human intracortical recordings, NeuroLens learns representations that improve decoding of abstract variables, including decisions and sentence meaning. In chronic mouse neural recordings during visual decision-making, these representations capture gradual transitions between learning stages and the progressive orthogonalization of neural states associated with different choices. They also reveal distinct timescales of cortical reorganization across tasks during learning. With multi-day pretraining, these representations also support stable decoding across days, including leading performance on the FALCON benchmark. Together, these findings support NeuroLens as a framework for tracking learning-related representational changes while maintaining stable decoding over long timescales.

title: PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation
authors: Yunji Kim, Yunseok Lee, Hyunwoo Seo, Jaerim Choi, Woojin Lee
abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) coordinate industrial equipment through sensor inputs and control commands. Evaluating LLM-generated PLC programs requires observing device and workpiece states to assess task completion and safety. We introduce PLCWorld, a closed-loop execution environment and benchmark coupling Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback. Grounded in control relations from industrial PLC programs and engineering documentation, PLCWorld contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs across Motion Control and Material Handling, with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope. It reports Task Success and Safety Violation separately. Execution Gap measures the fraction of cases with task failure or observed safety violation among those assigned to programs passing a common submission-profile and I/O check. Validation combines practitioner review, reference and alternative programs, 542 targeted counterexamples, alignment checks, and independent ST runtime comparisons. Across six LLMs and four adapted generation-and-verification workflows, direct GPT-5.5 achieves 83.96% Task Success on Easy cases but 24.51% on Hard cases. The workflows show no consistent plant-level gains, and failures persist after upstream acceptance. Our code is available at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/.

title: RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer
authors: Shenzhe Zhu, Chengxiao He, Jan Harder
abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.

title: Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation
authors: Jing Xie, Shouwei Ruan, Yubin Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Junwei Yang, Songchang Jin, Dianxi Shi
abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

title: BACAM: Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging for Multi-Turn Interaction
authors: Shuaitong Li, Baochen Xiong, Xiaoshan Yang, Xizhe Zheng, Yifan Xu, Jianhao Huang, Changsheng Xu
abstract: Model merging offers a way to integrate the capabilities of specialized experts, but existing agent merging methods typically require all of them to be available at once. We study continual agent merging, which integrates incoming experts sequentially without retaining previously merged experts. Yet merging in parameter space or feature subspaces does not ensure that the merged model acquires an incoming expert's behavior on interaction trajectories. Moreover, updates toward a new expert can disrupt the merged model's previously integrated interactive behavior. Therefore, we propose Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM), which learns parameter-wise merging gates from candidate-generated trajectories using expert-guided behavioral supervision. Task-level stability-plasticity control and tensor-level conflict-aware update budgets limit interference with existing capabilities while allowing new ones to be acquired. The learned gates are folded into the model weights without additional inference-time parameters. Across four interactive tasks - web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction - BACAM achieves an average success rate of 62.82%, exceeding the strongest evaluated merging baseline by 21.69 percentage points. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shuaitongli/BACAM.

title: Direction-Conditioned Policies for Online Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
authors: S K Swaminathan, Damiya Gondha, Theyanesh Eswaramoorthy Rajahkrishnan, Aritra Hazra
abstract: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) learns representations that estimate goal reachability, yet its policy remains conditioned on raw goals and therefore does not directly exploit the geometry encoded by its critic. We introduce Direction-Conditioned Policies (DCP), a method built around a small modification to CRL: DCP selects previously visited states as waypoints during online training and conditions the policy on their direction and distance in representation space. At deployment, DCP applies the same interface directly to the final goal, requiring neither waypoint selection nor planning. Across nine navigation and manipulation tasks, DCP attains higher final success rates than CRL on seven tasks and spends more time near the goal on seven. Ablations show that most of the gains come from conditioning on direction and distance, while the waypoints let DCP learn on every task, including those where the goal is rarely reached early in training. Controlled maze experiments further show that DCP captures shortest-path geometry more accurately and that the supplied direction causally influences the actor's behavior. Finally, we show that learned candidate generation improves goal reaching in two controlled mazes.

title: LeAVJEPA: A Minimalist Architecture for Audio-Visual Self-Supervised Learning
authors: Benjamin Robson, Santeri Mentu, Wenshuai Zhao, Arno Solin
abstract: Prior audio-visual self-supervised learning methods rely on mechanisms such as EMA target encoders, prediction heads, reconstruction decoders, and contrastive losses. We introduce LeAVJEPA, the first audio-visual encoder trained under LeJEPA's collapse-free objective. A single early-fusion Vision Transformer processes audio, video, and joint audio-video inputs. Modality dropout treats a missing modality as another view of the same event, making cross-modal alignment implicit in the objective. The model aligns global embeddings with modality-specific local embeddings, and SIGReg prevents representational collapse. A controlled ablation identifies modality dropout as the key mechanism for audio-visual alignment. Despite the architectural simplicity, LeAVJEPA reaches 36.0 mAP on AudioSet-20K and 91.3% accuracy on ESC-50 under frozen evaluation. After fine-tuning, it reaches 61.1% accuracy on VGGSound, and its embeddings support zero-shot audio-visual retrieval.

title: A Single-Loop, Constant-Batch First-Order Penalty Method for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization
authors: Xingyu Chen, Ming Yang, Quanqi Hu, Tianbao Yang
abstract: Recent advances in penalty-based methods for stochastic bilevel optimization (SBO) have eliminated the need for second-order derivative oracles. However, for stochastic nonconvex-strongly convex bilevel problems, existing first-order methods typically rely on nested loops and/or large batch sizes for attaining $O(\epsilon^{-6})$ or $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity under standard bounded-variance assumption or mean-square smoothness assumption. Achieving these rates with a single-loop penalty method and a constant batch size remains challenging due to a large penalty value needed for an accurate approximation. To address this challenge, we develop a stochastic SIngle-loop COnstant-Batch first-order penalty method (SICO) that combines two complementary ingredients. First, it performs one stochastic-gradient update per-iteration for both the original lower-level and penalized problems, with a projection that controls the separation between their iterates. Second, it applies an exponential moving average to stabilize the upper-level gradient estimator. We show that this combination achieves $ O(\epsilon^{-6}) $ sample complexity using only $O(1)$ stochastic-gradient samples per iteration under unbiased, bounded-variance stochastic gradients. Under the additional mean-square smoothness assumption on the lower-level stochastic gradients, the same algorithm improves the complexity to $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ also with $O(1)$ batch size. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to match the best-known convergence rate for fully first-order SBO methods using a single loop and a constant batch size. This result addresses an open problem posed in the literature.

title: What Frame-Level Labels Can and Cannot Do for Small-UAV Point Detection in Thermal Video
authors: Wonbin Son, Gyumum Choi, Junil Seo, Hyungjoon Kim
abstract: The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has increased the importance of image-based UAV detection. Learning-based detectors are trained on imagery and annotations, with annotation type determining the information available during training. We focus on learning localization from frame-level target presence/absence labels when sensor or scene changes make spatial annotations for additional training burdensome. We analyze the detection capability, learning behavior, and potential applications of an existing architecture for point detection of small UAVs, trained with presence/absence labels and requiring no external detector. The architecture freezes spatial features learned through classification and trains a readout with the same frame labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. On two thermal infrared datasets, CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410, we evaluate localization hit rates and detection rates under false-alarm constraints, analyze the effects of training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration, and compare with bounding-box detectors. We also explore potential applications on Airborne Object Tracking (AOT) using its visible-light imagery and frame labels. Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses, while readout training helped extract them consistently. Distributing similar label counts across more videos yielded higher localization hit rates, while synthesis effects varied by dataset and evaluation criterion. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints, and failures remained when target signals were weak relative to background variation and under cross-dataset transfer. These findings provide guidance on label allocation, spatial representations and readouts, synthesis, and false-alarm control.

title: The Labeling Problem in Hallucination Detection Benchmarks: An Empirical Evaluation
authors: Jorma Valjakka, Juhani Kivim\"aki, Juha Myll\"ari, Jukka K. Nurminen
abstract: In recent years, several methods for detecting when large language models (LLMs) hallucinate have been developed. These methods are often benchmarked with open-domain question answering (QA) datasets containing questions and corresponding short reference answers. First, an LLM is used to generate answers to questions within the QA dataset. Then, some automated labeling strategy is used to label these answers as hallucinated or not by comparing them with the reference answers in the dataset. This evaluation setting creates a methodological ambiguity between two criteria: reference faithfulness (whether the answer is fully supported by the reference) and factual correctness (whether the answer is free from contradictions and factually false specific claims). In practice, automated labelers may apply the former criterion even when the intended target is the latter. We study this potential criterion mismatch using 900 human-labeled question-answer pairs spanning three commonly used QA datasets and three generator models, with labels targeting answer-level factual correctness. We evaluate lexical similarity metrics, a reference-entailment NLI baseline, and seven LLM judges under controlled prompt variants as automated labelers. Our experiments reveal substantial disagreement both among automated labeling strategies and between these labels and human annotations. Many strategies also exhibit strong directional error biases, and for most judge-generator pairs, replacing a faithfulness-oriented prompt with a factual-correctness prompt improves agreement with human annotations and reduces false-positive dominance, indicating that automated hallucination labels depend strongly on how the target criterion is specified. Label-source choice should therefore be considered a fundamental part of benchmark design and made explicit, validated, and matched with the benchmark goal.

title: OSFP4: Joint Optimization of Diagonal Smoothing and Block Scales for NVFP4 Quantization
authors: Neriah Ben David, Ori Meir, Or Ordentlich
abstract: NVFP4 is an attractive datatype for large language model (LLM) inference, offering compact storage and native tensor-core acceleration. However, preserving accuracy using NVFP4 requires careful quantization. In this work we develop a novel quantization scheme called Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4 (OSFP4). For each linear projection it uses a diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize the squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4, taking into account the rounding procedure that is used (either round-to-nearest, or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). This requires performing joint optimization on the smoothing entries as well as the block scales, which is facilitated by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one. Experiments show that OSFP4 achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated competitors in the corresponding quantization settings, while retaining approximately 94-97\% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on the measured workloads. Our code is available in https://github.com/neriahbd/OSFP4

title: Open problem: Computing Bayes-Nash equilibrium in simple security games
authors: Vincent Conitzer
abstract: This is an open problem originally posed during the program "Economics and Computation" held in the Fall 2015 semester at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. It asks whether a (Bayes-)Nash equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time for Bayesian simple security games.

title: A Wasserstein Trust-Region Method for Smooth Potential-Interaction Energies
authors: You Wan, Ting Gao, Jinqiao Duan, Jie Sun
abstract: Finding low-energy particle configurations and approximating probability distributions both lead to minimizing potential-interaction energies in Wasserstein space. Second-order information can speed up minimizing these possibly nonconvex energies, but a quadratic model is accurate only near the current measure. We introduce a Wasserstein trust-region (WTR) method for smooth, possibly nonconvex energies of this type. Each iteration transports the current measure $\rho$ along a displacement field $s$, producing $(\mathrm{Id}+s)_\#\rho$. The field approximately minimizes a quadratic model built from the second variation of the energy, subject to $\|s\|_{L^2(\rho)}\le\Delta$, using a truncated conjugate-gradient method. The ratio of actual to predicted decrease determines step acceptance and updates the trust-region radius. Under a lower energy bound and globally bounded Hessians of the potential and interaction kernel, we prove that the objective is nonincreasing, the Wasserstein-gradient norms converge to zero, and an $\varepsilon$-stationary iterate is reached within $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations, rejected ones included. If the potential is quadratically coercive, every weak accumulation point is stationary. For empirical measures, WTR is an ordinary trust-region method in the particle positions, and its complexity bound does not depend on the number of particles provided the initial energy exceeds its infimum by a bounded amount. For $2048$ and $4096$ particles with Gaussian pair repulsion in a two-dimensional harmonic trap, WTR reaches the gradient tolerance $2\times10^{-4}$ a median $1.40$ times faster than L-BFGS. For equal-weight integration rules on two non-Gaussian targets, WTR reaches an integration error of $10^{-4}$ about $1.8$ times faster than L-BFGS and $1.3$ times faster than a Krylov trust-region solver.

title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation
authors: Yuxiang Fu, Qi Yan, Zike Wu, Yongxing Zhang, Purang Abolmaesumi, Lele Wang, Renjie Liao
abstract: Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher's dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, orchestration of multiple objectives, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity of the teacher model. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network, which greatly simplifies the distribution matching distillation pipeline. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256$\times$256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. On text-to-image distillation tasks, our method also enable fast high-fidelity generation with no image data required. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/.

title: FLoRa: Flight-Assisted Data Collection from Duty Cycling LoRa Nodes under Energy Constraints
authors: Naresh Babu Kakarla, V. Mahendran
abstract: Data collection using Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) is challenging when LoRa IoT Devices (IoTDs) duty-cycle to conserve battery. Under energy constraints, a UAV must decide which IoTDs to visit, in what order, where to hover, and how many times to probe each node, while time-based data freshness decays. Tractably solving this problem requires a multi-level optimization architecture: discrete combinatorial optimization for routing, continuous global optimization for spatial positioning, and sequential decision-making under uncertainty. We propose FLoRa, a Flight-assisted LoRa data collection architecture using Simulated Annealing (SA) for path planning, Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) for hover positioning, and Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) for probing IoTDs. To quantify collection utility from duty-cycling nodes, we introduce the Value of Information for Pull-based systems (VIP), a metric that rewards fresh data and penalizes failed probes, imposing well-posedness and preventing indefinite probing when an IoTD is off. Tracking hard battery constraints on every POMDP sample path requires state augmentation, worsening the curse of dimensionality. For tractability, SA and CMA-ES work on the hard battery constraints, while at the POMDP layer we relax them into soft average constraints via Lagrangian relaxation. Since solving the network-wide POMDP is computationally complex, we decompose it into node-level POMDPs by approximating inter-node time dependency using a forward-decomposition technique. Evaluation shows that FLoRa outperforms greedy, metaheuristic, and deep reinforcement learning baselines, as well as recent UAV data collection methods, by 27.8-76.1% in total expected VIP, 23.5-45.7% in node coverage, and 23.3-54.4% in successful collections.

title: Fully Interpretable Minimal Transformers: From Geometry to Algorithm
authors: Raneem Mahajne, Toviah Moldwin
abstract: We present a framework for building and interpreting minimal transformer models. By constraining a transformer's embedding dimension and head size to 2, we enable full two-dimensional visualization of its internal representations. Embeddings, query/key/value transforms, attention outputs, residual streams, and decision boundaries can all be seen directly. Our central claim is that the learned geometry implies an algorithm. The arrangement of points and boundaries in R^2 can be read as a step-by-step procedure. We train a transformer on a simple task where it must produce the most recently observed even number whenever the '+' operator appears in a sequence of digits. Once trained, we visually walk through every step of the transformer's computation. We show how the model embeds the tokens and their respective positions in the sequence, transforms them via the Q, K, and V matrices, uses the dot product between the Q and K representations to form the attention matrix, and uses the attention matrix to select values that move the representation of each input token embedding to the region of the domain of the output layer that will correctly predict the next token. We introduce a suite of interpretability visualizations that make the algorithmic interpretation of this procedure explicit. Our framework offers a pedagogical and experimental testbed to explore how transformers use information geometry to implement next-token prediction.

title: EASE: Entropy-Adaptive Distribution Shaping for Evading AI-generated Text Detectors
authors: Jicheng Zhou, Kahim Wong, Jialong Wang, Jiantao Zhou
abstract: AI-generated text (AIGT) detection can be sensitive to the decoding choices of the source large language model (LLM). We observe that perturbing next-token logits or adjusting sampling temperature can reduce detection performance, providing a clear signal of detector vulnerability to decoding-time distribution changes. Building on this observation, we propose EASE (Entropy-Adaptive Distribution Shaping for Evasion), a training-free and detector-agnostic framework for evading AIGT detectors. EASE computes predictive entropy directly from the source LLM's next-token distribution and uses it to adapt both logit perturbation and sampling temperature, without detector feedback or model fine-tuning. Experiments across three source LLMs and multiple detectors demonstrate consistent reductions in detection performance, with negligible degradation in text quality and negligible inference overhead.

title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
authors: Kamile Dementaviciute, Julija Vaitonyte, Tijl De Bie
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $\rho = 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

title: Optimal Multi-Item Auctions with I.I.D. Values
authors: Boyu Liu, Zhengyang Liu, Zihe Wang
abstract: We study revenue-maximizing auctions for additive buyers whose item values are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) draws from a finite distribution, under dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC) and ex-post individual rationality (IR). For any two-point distribution and any numbers of buyers and items, we construct an explicit deterministic auction that achieves the optimal expected revenue, even among randomized DSIC, ex-post IR mechanisms. Furthermore, its expected revenue can be computed in polynomial time. In contrast, we show that the problem becomes intractable once the number of support points is part of the input: even with a single buyer, and even with two items, both constructing an optimal mechanism and computing the optimal revenue are $\sharpP$-hard.

title: Ambient Discrete Diffusion: Using the Wrong Data at the Right Time for Data Efficient Learning
authors: Julian Kleutgens, Mauricio Tec, Claudio Battiloro, Francesca Dominici, Giannis Daras
abstract: We introduce RefineMix, a framework for training discrete diffusion models under severe data scarcity, a common constraint in scientific applications. RefineMix uses out-of-distribution data at selected diffusion times to improve generalization without biasing the sampling distribution. Although this strategy has been explored in continuous diffusion, discrete diffusion presents a distinct challenge: unlike Gaussian noise, masking preserves domain information in surviving tokens, limiting the use of related data at high noise levels. At low noise levels, however, the domains effectively disjoint supports become an advantage, allowing the model to learn from both in-domain and out-of-distribution data without biasing the sampler. We formalize these intuitions and provide a theoretical analysis for the proposed method. Experimentally, across five domain-shift settings, RefineMix matches or outperforms in-domain finetuning and data mixing. For protein sequence generation, finetuning with just 197 in-domain examples nearly doubles the fraction of generated proteins that are simultaneously novel, foldable, and in-family compared to standard finetuning.

title: DistressBench: Evaluating Multi-Dimensional Crisis Support in Large Language Models
authors: Drew Rein, Patrick Oathout, Vishal Kumar, Udari Madhushani Sehwag
abstract: Language models have been adopted faster than evaluation practices that reliably assess their risks, and a growing share of use is affective rather than informational. Within that traffic users disclose suicide and self-harm (SSH) crises. Existing safety benchmarks score models primarily on refusal, but refusal is not the desired behavior here; the conversation requires a substantive supportive response. We introduce DistressBench, 718 English conversations with clinician-authored user turns spanning 23 SSH subcategories, each paired with a task-specific rubric of weighted atomic criteria across seven dimensions of crisis support and a clinician reference response. A model's score is the share of clinician-specified, scenario-weighted criteria its reply satisfies. The best of 25 frontier models satisfies 88.4% of weighted criteria and the median model 71.4%, against 98.7% for clinician references scored on the same criteria. Pooled across all 25 models, in 35.3% of conversations where a model satisfied every criterion for recognizing the crisis, it missed at least one clinician-specified resource action; most of these still offer some route to human help, but 18% offer none in the final reply and 5.5% none at all. The shortfall concentrates in the dimensions requiring the model to act rather than withhold. The two largest deficits are already achieved by a deployed model: de-escalation reaches 74.6% in the strongest model against a median of 46.0%, and safety disclaimers 84.6% against 8.3%. Multi-turn conversations score below single-turn ones (68.5% against 74.2%). We release the corpus, rubrics, judge calibration labels, and a companion annex of 20 long-horizon red-team transcripts. These results argue for evaluating crisis safety on the care a model delivers rather than on what it declines to say, and for treating de-escalation and resource routing as deployment requirements.

title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators
authors: Sevan Brodjian, Michael Hobley, Pietro Perona
abstract: A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model acts as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. We test two kinds of state mappings, both fit from latent states paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the simulator-to-latent mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even when steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, in ways decodability does not predict. In Othello, each simplification of the rules lowers editability. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. Editability across layers suggests that the Othello model compresses its history into a board partway through the network, while the Rayworld model shifts its recent frames and then refines a rendering of the next frame. The inverse map succeeds by approximating this partial rendering. We relate both outcomes to the causal state of computational mechanics, the minimal summary of its history a model must keep to predict optimally, which may not align with the simulator. Guided by this view, we change how the Rayworld model is trained and make its state more simulator-like.

title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Linli Yao, Shicheng Li, Xu Sun, Haoli Bai, Xiaohui Li
abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
authors: Zhengxi Li, Junyi Zhou, Qiyuan Zhang, Chuhan Wu, Fuyuan Lyu, Le Tian, Xiao Zhou, Xue Liu, Chen Ma, Yufei Wang
abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.

title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics Toward Long-Horizon Rollouts in World Models
authors: Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. We measure rollout collapse on the data, with four ratios of the rollout to the truth, on five environments learned from pixels: conservative and actuated pendulums, a mass-spring, a two-body system and a cart pole. With the encoder and latent state held fixed, an MLP and a transformer predictor contract the rollout on every environment, while LeHami's rollouts do not merge. LeHami is the most accurate of the three at long horizons, in position on four of the five environments and in velocity on three, while at short horizons the free predictors are more accurate on two of the five. The learned flow also integrates at unseen sub-frame step sizes and, run backward with the recorded actions, recovers earlier frames as well as it predicts later ones. LeWM, with a richer three-frame encoder of its own, is more accurate on four of the five, which suggests incorporating a richer encoder within LeHami in future work. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.

title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
authors: Chen Huang, Yiyang Zhang, Yuhao Wu, Yang Deng, Wenxuan Zhang
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.

title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
authors: Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, Chenran Cai, Bin Liang, Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong
abstract: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.

title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
authors: Bryce Grant, Peng Wang
abstract: Prior research into interpretability does not test whether a representation stays consistent under paraphrasing. Each pair of paraphrases can be thought of as a local witness that two activations should be the same. From these local witnesses we can build a cellular sheaf on the paraphrase graph. The question of what is consistent under paraphrasing can be answered by the Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ given a frozen model. No training required. Our kernel $H^0$ gives us a content subspace. We show that with only 20 dims the kernel outperforms the subspace that LEACE retains with all dims on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval by $+17.1$\,pp on average across 8 models. By constraining all paraphrases of a fact together we see an additional increase of $+6.5$\,pp. Our spectral complement shows us where the causal influence is concentrated. Ablating the coordinates that vary the most when paraphrased (which approximates ablating the spectral complement at the coordinate level) leads to $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ larger changes in model outputs compared to ablating coordinates with matched per-coordinate variability. We find this across 9 models from 124M to 13B params. By stacking layers we can create a grid which has $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles. The harmonic mass derived from the model varies by nearly 3 orders of magnitude between the 6 architectures. It also tracks the order of steering fragility (Spearman's $\rho = 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The kernel, its spectral complement and the harmonic mass all come from the same paraphrase graph. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/.

title: Good human thinking populates AI's semantic blind spots
authors: Kibum Moon, Dan R. Johnson, Kostadin Kushlev, Oded Kleinmintz, Benjamin Lira, Indre Viskontas, James C. Kaufman, Roger E. Beaty, Nirav Patel, Emily Wenger, Angela L. Duckworth, Adam E. Green
abstract: AI-generated outputs tend to be more similar (homogenized) than human ideas. Does the human heterogeneity that extends beyond AI homogenization reflect valuable thinking that AI misses, or bad human ideas that AI avoids? We quantified how much an individual response expands an idea space beyond recurring clusters of ideas, enabling us to identify human responses located in AI's "semantic blind spots" (regions AI sparsely covers). Across three large samples (college admissions essays, alternative uses of objects, and interpersonal problem solving), human ideas in AI blind spots predicted higher academic achievement and performed as well or better on creativity, quality, and effectiveness. In contrast to humans, when AI expanded idea space, the association with creativity weakened or reversed. AI blind spots persisted across 66 diverse models and were not resolved by human-AI collaboration. Thinking "outside the bots" does not appear to reflect low-performing human variation that AI can safely omit.

title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
authors: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge
abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Miao Li, Hanyang Jiang, Hengyu Fu, Baihe Huang, Yating Liu, Yuhang Cai, Changkun Guan, Zhongzhu Chen, Jiecheng Lu, Michael A. Boateng, Pascal Van Hentenryck
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
authors: Yu Mi, Licheng Pan, Jiayi Zhu, Qirui Liu, Yitong Qiao, Changtong Xu, Tao Wei, Fei Sun, Zhixuan Chu, Kui Ren
abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.

title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
authors: Cheng Hua, Taro Tsuchiya, Nicolas Christin, Giulia Fanti
abstract: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 63.6% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 79.8% of runs containing violations. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.

title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

title: JockeyBench: The Racing Analyst's Last Exam
authors: Zhongwei Xie, Xingsu Li, Jingqiao Yu, Zihao Wang, Hong ChiTat, Zhaowei Wang, Weizhi Du, Yuxuan Liu, Huihao Jing, Jiaxin Bai, Yangqiu Song
abstract: Evaluating LLM agents in noisy sequential forecasting is challenging: strong performance may reflect a capable initial predictor rather than successful online revision, while accurate forecasts may still fail to deliver economic value after costs and market frictions. Existing benchmarks rarely isolate revision gains, compare reusable model-written predictors with direct LLM forecasting on the same tasks, or assess forecast quality alongside research costs and realized returns. To address these gaps, we introduce JockeyBench, a leakage-controlled replay benchmark built from 12 years of Japanese horse-racing records. Agents acquire evidence at a cost and seal probabilistic forecasts before outcomes are revealed. To isolate the effect of revision, we pair each adaptive code-as-policy agent with a frozen copy of its initial predictor. We also compare code-as-policy, which executes reusable prediction programs, with LLM-as-policy, which forecasts each race directly. We evaluate 29 models on 324 races. The strongest initial predictors outperform a conditional-logit baseline trained on 20,730 races. The two top-ranked models retain their initial predictors throughout evaluation. Revision helps weaker predictors correct overconfidence, but updates driven by noisy outcomes can hurt performance. Code-as-policy generally produces more accurate forecasts at lower research cost, while models that struggle to write reliable predictors benefit from forecasting directly with LLM-as-policy. Yet all 29 models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, have negative mean returns in retrospective settlement. JockeyBench thus offers a demanding testbed for current LLM agents.

title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
authors: Shiv Muthupandiyan, Tolga H. Dur, Mac Walker, Steph Suddell, Timo Flesch, Mahmoud Ghanem, Giles Harper-Donnelly, Sophie Rose, Jasper G\"otting, Coleman Breen, Jake Pencharz
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data or generated outputs. We evaluated selected functionalities of a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, restricted here to unconditional protein-backbone generation, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools may have been included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-weight coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability on some tasks, though no clear reproduction of the most complex tool we evaluate. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers may need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of selected functionalities, based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or weaken dual-use managed access strategies.

title: FOLD: Position-Free Far Memory with Local Order for Long-Context Speculative Decoding
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Zhilin Zhao, Xiao Yang
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.

title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
authors: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so the probability that a loop survives $m$ more repetitions is, under any sampler, a product of per-step continuation probabilities computable from one forward pass. A lock, where this probability stays exactly one, is its limiting case. Pure sampling never locks; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis shows a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 61% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 0.2% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 199 loops that survive DRY, on six models, have $g\le 7$. We propose a count term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window, and closes this blind spot. Added to DRY (DRY-C), it cuts loops in 1,800 structured generations on five models from 167 to 34, and loops reaching the length limit from 150 to 0, with reasoning accuracy and item coverage on par with DRY. DRY's own length term costs 2.5 to 14.2 points of accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500; used in its place, the count term keeps the default sampler's accuracy and leaves one of the 1,800 generations at the limit.

title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
authors: Zixuan Dong, Yanghai Wang, Hanyan Bian, Jiaxi Tao, Junze Li, Jiadong Wang, Xinyu Che, Lin Liu, Baoyun Peng, Xiaodong Wang, Jiaheng Liu
abstract: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.

title: CIS-Transolver: A neural operator for fine-scale automotive aerodynamic flow prediction
authors: Jianglong Liu, Zhicheng Zhu, Jia Hao, Liangyue Jia, Wenxuan He
abstract: Automotive aerodynamic optimization requires accurate predictions of both vehicle-scale pressure and velocity distributions and local fine-scale spatial variations near complex geometries. Spectral bias in neural operators hinders the fitting of high-frequency spatial components, limiting fine-scale flow prediction. To mitigate this bias, we propose CIS-Transolver, an automotive flow prediction method that combines spatial representations of local multiscale variations with cross-layer state updates. Geometric moments of orders zero through two encode local feature increments and their spatial correlations, while current observations are combined with states retained from preceding layers to form cross-layer memory. This memory is fed back through the value branch of Physics-Attention at each layer, allowing local fine-scale variations to continually inform the prediction of the overall flow field. CIS-Transolver is evaluated on three public automotive flow datasets, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, for predicting vehicle surface pressure and surrounding three-dimensional pressure and velocity fields. Across all five prediction tasks, it achieves the lowest mean relative L2 errors and corresponding high-frequency spectral errors among the methods compared. Relative to the best-performing baseline for each task and metric, the relative reductions, averaged across the five tasks, are 8.72% and 16.06%, respectively. Spatial increment analysis further demonstrates improved prediction of local pressure and velocity variations. These improvements in overall flow accuracy and high-frequency prediction provide more accurate flow information for automotive aerodynamic performance assessment and design optimization.

title: How Wet-Biased Datasets Shape the Training and Mislead the Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
authors: Christoph Metzl, Stefan Kapsreiter, Kianusch Vahid Yousefnia, Virginia Poli, Richard M\"uller, Frank Kr\"uger, Tobias B\"olle
abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically that the same target-dependent selection, applied to the training set, tilts the conditional distribution learned by an ideal generative model by exactly the factor that such an evaluation rewards. We test both evaluation and training effects with a satellite-to-radar diffusion model in a controlled experiment that crosses wet-biased and uniform sampling of the training and of the test set. The evaluation effect appears in full: the same model looks under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predicts light rain on a deployment-consistent one, whichever way it was trained. Inverse probability weighting recovers the deployment scores from the wet-biased set. The training effect is real but partial: the model trained on wet-biased data forecasts more rain than its uniformly trained counterpart, yet remains far from calibrated even on a test set drawn like its training set, and gains skill for rain at a modest cost in calibration. Wet-biased training is thus a trade-off, not an error. Using classifier-free guidance as an example of a tuned quantity, we show how this misdirects model development: most scores on the wet-biased test set favor the largest guidance scale, whereas calibration, frequency bias, and a threshold-weighted proper score on the deployment-consistent set favor the smallest.

title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
authors: Qian Xie, Yueli He, Wenyue Hua, Sripad Karne, Armaan Agrawal, Nikos Pagonas, Eugene Wu, Kostis Kaffes, Tianyi Peng, Nairen Cao
abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation.
